title: Sonata
program_note:
This Clarinet Sonata was begun in February, 1989, and was completed in June of the same year.  The revised version was begun in September, 1990 and was completed in October, 1990, and was retranscribed in August, 2010.  Most of the material for the outer movements was drawn from sketches for a chamber opera tentatively entitled Medea.  The middle movement draws, in part, on sketches for an unaccompanied clarinet work.

The first movement is quite virtuosic, but the overall emotional feeling is one of anguish and pain, rather than flash and brilliance.  In measures 4 through 12, and again in m.53, the clarinet is called upon to bend the pitch up or down a quarter step.  In mm. 73-80, the tuplets in the clarinet part need not be "scientific":  the performer must simply insure that all of the notes fit into the beat, as written.  The quarter-note pulse, however, must remain clear.  The piano part from mm.89 to 94 is meant to be a recollection that is painful to complete; not until the clarinet takes over in m.95 does the main idea get underway again, only to be sharply terminated.

The second movement should have a somewhat jazzy or at least jaunty feel throughout.  In the opening, the jauntiness should come from the off-beat impulses, usually every three sixteenth-notes.  The clarinet introduction, from mm.2-9, should introduce some metrical ambiguity, but once the piano starts in at m.10, the pulse of the quarter-note should never be lost to the listener.  From mm.23-32, the more traditionally jazzy feel, with the walking bass-line and off-beat chordal accents, tries to break into the fortspinnung of the opening, finally succeeding at m.33.  Throughout this section, all triplets should have the feel of a very lazy duplet.  The grace notes should be short, but not clipped; together with the following quarter notes, they should sound like the B'doom B'doom of a walking bass-line or a jazz quartet.  Similarly, the chords in the right hand of the piano should have the feel of the jazz pianist, perhaps like Thelonius Monk.  The tremolos in the piano part in mm.57-58 are meant to be similar to the trumpet section trills in big bands, and can be added in at other places.  Similarly, the clarinet can add in shakes or warbles wherever appropriate to the context.

The last movement should sound extremely romantic — perhaps reminiscent of one of the middle movements of Brahms' first clarinet sonata.  An easy rubato is called for throughout.  The tempo accelerations and decelerations given in the first eight bars are meant as suggestions.  Although the music slows down at points, every effort should be made to keep a flowing feeling moving throughout, until the “free cadenza.”  Although mm.89-93 are notated metrically, the performers are invited to take this section as they please,  merely preserving the basic relationships of short and long notes.

The total duration of the work is approximately fourteen and a half minutes.  The durations of each movement are as follows:  6:00, 3:00, and 5:15-5:30.  The performers are meant to have a degree of freedom in interpreting this work:  tempos are approximate, and pedaling and articulation changes, for example, can be used if appropriate.  The score is written for Clarinet in Bb.

David S. Lefkowitz

12 November 1990Philadelphia,  PA
